The kernel ideal of a morphism from a reduced scheme is radical, so the scheme-theoretic closure defining the strict transform is reduced.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.ker_comap_ι_eq_ker_morphismRestrict: Take an affine open in the restricted target and identify it with its image in the ambient target. Its inverse images under the restricted map and the original map likewise identify via the open inclusion of the restricted source. The corresponding square of section maps commutes. The horizontal identifications of the section rings are isomorphisms, so an ambient section lies in the original kernel exactly when its restricted section lies in the new kernel. The affine charts therefore give equality of the two ideal sheaves.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.ker_comap_ι_eq_ker_of_isIso_comp: Restriction along the open inclusion gives the kernel of the restricted morphism. The new morphism is obtained from it by precomposition with an isomorphism, which preserves the kernel.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.ker_eq_ker_of_isIso_comp: Precomposing with an isomorphism changes the induced maps on sections by isomorphisms on their targets. These preserve exactly which sections map to zero, so the kernel ideal sheaf is unchanged.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.ker_ideal_eq_ker_app: For a quasi-compact morphism, the kernel ideal on an affine target open is the kernel of the homomorphism from its section ring to the sections over its inverse image.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.ker_morphismRestrict_subschemeι: Restricting the closed immersion to the open gives the base change of the closed immersion by the open inclusion. The pullback closed immersion is defined by the pulled-back ideal, so this ideal is its kernel.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.ker_ι_preimage_comp_subschemeι_eq_ker_co: The restriction of the closed immersion factors through an isomorphism to the closed subscheme of the restricted ideal. The equation for restricting a morphism identifies the two ambient maps after that isomorphism. Precomposition with the isomorphism leaves the kernel unchanged.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.quasiCompact_of_isInducing: The image of the inverse image of a quasi-compact open is a subset of that open. In a locally Noetherian scheme it is therefore quasi-compact. An inducing map reflects quasi-compactness from the image to the inverse-image space, proving quasi-compactness of the morphism.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.quasiCompact_strictTransformι_of_isLocal: The strict-transform immersion is a composite of an open immersion and a closed immersion. Both induce the subspace topology and so does their composite. Since the ambient target is locally Noetherian, the quasi-compactness criterion for an inducing morphism applies.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.range_comp_eq_image_range: A point belongs to the range of the composite exactly when it is the image under the second map of some value of the first map. This gives equality with the image of the first range.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.strictTransformImmersion_eq_strictTransf: Both constructions are the same composite of the open inclusion away from the pulled-back center and the closed immersion of the pulled-back subscheme.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.strictTransform_congr_of_comap_ι_eq: The restricted kernel formula computes the strict transform using only the ideal restricted to the complement of the center. The two restrictions agree by hypothesis, hence so do the two strict transforms.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.strictTransform_eq_ker_restrict: The complement of the pulled-back center support is the inverse image of the center complement. Restrict the total-transform subscheme to this open. Its ideal is the pullback of the original ideal restricted to the center complement, by the commuting restriction square. The strict-transform kernel is consequently the kernel of this restricted closed immersion followed by the ambient open inclusion.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.strictTransform_eq_ker_strictTransformι: The strict-transform ideal is the ideal of the scheme-theoretic image of the open immersion into the pulled-back subscheme followed by its ambient inclusion. This is the kernel ideal sheaf of the displayed immersion.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.strictTransform_top: Pullback of the unit ideal is the unit ideal. The total-transform ideal is contained in the strict-transform ideal, so the latter contains the unit ideal and equals it.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.strictTransformι_eq_ι_comp_subschemeι: The strict-transform immersion first includes the open away from the exceptional support into the pulled-back subscheme and then includes that closed subscheme into the ambient scheme.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.support_strictTransform_eq_closure_preim: The support of the kernel ideal of the quasi-compact immersion is the closure of its point image. That image is the support of the pulled-back subscheme ideal intersected with the complement of the pulled-back center support. Both pulled-back supports are inverse images. Taking their difference commutes with inverse image, giving the asserted closure.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.support_strictTransform_eq_closure_sdiff: Replace each pulled-back support by the inverse image of its original support. The difference of the two inverse images is the inverse image of the difference, so the previous closure description gives the equality.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.coe_complComapSupport: Passing to underlying sets, the points of this open are exactly the points outside the support of the pulled-back center ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.complComapSupport_eq: The open under consideration is defined as the complement of the support of the center ideal pulled back along the given morphism.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.strictTransform_comap_complComapSupport_: The strict transform is the scheme-theoretic closure of the pulled-back closed subscheme restricted to the complement of the exceptional support. Equivalently, its ideal is the kernel of the restricted closed immersion followed by the open inclusion. Restricting that kernel back along the open inclusion gives the kernel of the restricted closed immersion itself. This is precisely the restriction of the pulled-back ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.strictTransform_comap_of_comap_center_eq: The pulled-back center ideal on the new source is the unit ideal, so its support is empty. Since support is preserved by inverse image, the morphism factors through the complement of the center support on the blowup. On that open the strict-transform ideal agrees with the pulled-back ideal. Pull the equality back along the factorization.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.comap_eq_ker_pullback_fst: The pullback ideal is defined by the base change of the closed subscheme inclusion. Its ideal is the kernel of the projection from that pullback to the source, giving the identity.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdealSheafIterate_congr_of_eq_of_eq: Identify the two equal structural morphisms and the two equal ideals. The resulting derivative iterates are formed with the same base algebra and input on every affine open, so they agree.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_etale_maxContactIdeal_comparison: The order locus is closed in a scheme quasi-compact over the field, so it is quasi-compact. For each point choose a local comparison. The two images of its étale maps are open, and their intersection contains the point. These intersections cover the order locus, so finitely many suffice. Apply the finite-cover construction to their comparison schemes.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_etale_maxContactIdeal_comparison_: Take the finite disjoint union of the affine comparison schemes and define each global map by its specified restriction on every summand. The union is affine, and both maps are étale because this holds on the summands. Its structure map to the field is locally of finite type and quasi-compact. The assumed cover by common ranges gives both range containments. The maps to the field agree on each summand, and the pullbacks of the given ideals, hypersurfaces, and boundary agree on each summand, hence globally. Pullback of the maximal-contact ideal to each summand commutes with its derivative iterate, so the maximal-contact closed subscheme restricts to the corresponding local one. The two maps agree there by the local comparisons, which proves equality on the whole maximal-contact subscheme.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.hom_ext_of_opens_cover: The open inclusions form a cover because every point lies in one of the given opens. Scheme morphisms are determined locally on the source, and the two morphisms agree when restricted to each member of the cover. They therefore agree globally.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.iUnion_range_sigmaι_base_eq_univ: Every point of a coproduct of schemes comes from a point of one of the summands. Thus it lies in the range of that summand’s inclusion, and the union of the ranges is the whole space.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.idealSheafData_eq_of_forall_comap_eq: For each point choose a preimage in one of the open immersions. Its stalk map is an isomorphism. The equal pulled-back ideals give equal extensions of the original stalk ideals along that isomorphism. Transporting back gives equality at the original point. Equality of all stalk ideals gives equality of the ideal sheaves.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.ideal_eq_of_map_eq_of_leftInverse: Extend each side of the equality along the left inverse. Successive extensions equal extension along their composite, which is the identity on the original ring. This recovers the original ideals on both sides.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.subschemeι_comp_eq_of_forall_sigmaι_coma: The inverse images in the closed subscheme of the summand opens cover it. On one such inverse image, the map to the ambient coproduct factors through the corresponding summand by the open immersion property. Together with the map to the closed subscheme, this gives a map to their fiber product. That fiber product maps to the closed subscheme defined by the pulled-back ideal, since its projection kills that ideal. Thus the two morphisms agree on this open by the equality assumed on the pulled-back closed subscheme. The local equalities give the equality on the whole closed subscheme.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.appLE_topIso_hom_eq_appTop: Factor the section map through the open subscheme using the given factorization of the morphism. The section map of the open inclusion is the inverse of the stated section identification. These two maps cancel. The remaining map on the whole source and target opens is the global sections map of the factor through the open subscheme.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.chartPullbackFstStalkMap_eq_snd_of_coord: The fiber-product compatibility says that both maps agree modulo the maximal ideal and on the field, and that the difference in one chart is confined to its distinguished coordinate. The shift is the first image of the difference of the two distinguished germs. It lies in the maximal ideal by locality, and the given homomorphism kills it because it kills both of those germs after the first map. Apply the coordinate-shift difference result to its kernel ideal. The difference of the two maps on every element lies in that kernel, which gives equality after the homomorphism.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.chartPullbackStalkMap_compat: The fiber-product equation makes the pullbacks of corresponding chart coordinates equal on global sections. Taking germs gives the coordinate equalities at the chosen point. The two projections have the same structural map to the field, so they also agree on the structural scalars. The lift from the spectrum of the residue field has the same composite with both projections. Thus the two stalk images of any element become equal after the induced map to the stalk of the residue field spectrum. Their difference maps to zero in a nonzero ring, so it lies in the maximal ideal of the fiber-product stalk.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.chartsAgreeAt_of_coord_eq_of_germ_mem: Agreement at the point can be checked by requiring the differences of coordinate germs to lie in the maximal ideal. At all unaltered indices the coordinates agree, so the difference is zero. At the distinguished index both germs lie in the maximal ideal, and so does their difference. The same memberships hold on the open subscheme under the canonical section identifications, giving the agreement condition.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.coordIdeal_eq_of_coord_eq: Use the canonical section identification to regard the selected coordinates as global sections of the affine chart domain. All corresponding coordinates agree there. The two coordinate ideals are generated by these same global sections, so they agree.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.coordTop_topIso_eq_coord: The ambient section called the chart coordinate is defined by transporting the chart’s global section along the canonical identification of sections of the open. Applying that identification gives the stated coordinate.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.eqToHom_comp_stalkMap_congr: Identify the two equal morphisms. They induce the same maps on stalks, and the given identifications of the image point transport the same source stalk to the same ring. The two resulting composites agree.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.eqToHom_comp_stalkMap_germ: Identify the target point with the image of the source point. Pulling back the germ of a section along the stalk map is the germ of its pulled-back section. Restricting to the indicated source open does not change this germ, which gives the formula.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.eqToHom_comp_stalkMap_mem_maximalIdeal: After identifying the target point with the image point, the map is the stalk map of a scheme morphism. It is local and reflects units. A nonunit in the target stalk thus maps to a nonunit in the source stalk, which is the desired maximal-ideal membership.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_opens_chartPullback_eq_of_mem_max: The coordinates give agreement of the charts at the point and hence a point of their fiber product. Maximal-contact invariance and the shift calculation give equality of the two pulled-back stalk ideals there. This stalk equality extends to an open neighborhood by finite generation. The fiber-product point also lies in the support of the pulled-back maximal-contact ideal. Choose its point in that closed subscheme. The two projections restricted to the spectrum of its stalk agree because both distinguished coordinates vanish on the subscheme. Spread this morphism equality to an open neighborhood in the subscheme. Lift that neighborhood to an ambient open by the closed immersion and intersect it with the neighborhood of stalk equality. On the intersection the restrictions of the input ideals agree by their stalks, and the projections agree on the maximal-contact subscheme. The two distinguished coordinate ideals have equal pullbacks by the fiber-product equations. For any set of indices omitting the distinguished one, the charts already share the corresponding sections and therefore give equal coordinate ideals downstairs.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_preimage_eq_of_isClosedImmersion: A closed immersion gives its source the subspace topology of its image. Every open of the source is therefore the inverse image of an open of the ambient scheme. Choose that ambient open.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.fromSpecStalk_comp_eq_of_stalkMap_eq: The point equalities identify the target stalks of the two composites with the same stalk. The hypothesis then says their induced ring maps are equal on every element, so the maps agree. Functoriality of the canonical morphism from the spectrum of a stalk rewrites each scheme composite as the spectrum of its stalk map followed by the same canonical morphism. These are equal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.fromSpecStalk_comp_subschemeι_chartPullb: Choose an affine neighborhood of the fiber-product point inside the inverse image of the original chart. Both distinguished coordinate germs map to zero under the first projection followed by the stalk map to the maximal-contact subscheme because both sections belong to its defining maximal-contact ideal. The coordinate-shift comparison then identifies the two composites on every element of the original stalk. The correspondence with morphisms from the spectrum of the stalk gives the claimed equality of scheme maps.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.germ_topIso_inv_mem_maximalIdeal: The ambient section and its transported section on the open subscheme have corresponding germs. Indeed the inclusion pullback and the inverse section identification agree, and germ formation commutes with restriction. If the transported germ were a unit, the point would belong to its basic open. This is the inverse image of the original basic open and would make the original germ a unit. The given maximal-ideal membership rules this out.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.map_le_map_and_sub_mem_of_etaleChart_coo: The chart’s affine section ring is formally étale over its polynomial coordinate ring. The stalk is a localization of that section ring and is again formally étale over the polynomial ring by composition. Its coordinate functions are the germs of the chart coordinates and its constants are the structural field elements. Thus the hypotheses on the stalk maps are exactly those of the algebraic coordinate-shift result, which gives both conclusions.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.map_le_map_and_sub_mem_of_etaleCoordinat: Use the partial derivation in the shifted coordinate direction. It sends that coordinate to one and the other coordinates and field constants to zero. The Taylor expansion in the image of the shift agrees with the second map modulo every power of the maximal ideal on the polynomial generators. At truncation length one this follows from the shift lying in the maximal ideal. For longer truncations the expansion on each variable has only its constant and linear terms, which give the stated coordinates exactly. Formal unramifiedness and agreement modulo the maximal ideal extend this comparison to the full algebra. If the shift belongs to an ideal whose product with the derivative ideal of the input is contained in the input, induction puts each shift power times the corresponding iterated derivative back in the input. The Taylor ideal-containment result gives the first conclusion. The Taylor difference criterion gives the second, since every positive-order term contains the image of the shift.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.map_stalkMap_stalkIdeal_eq: Identify the image point with the specified point. Their stalk rings and stalk ideals then coincide, and transport along the point equality becomes the identity. Both sides extend the same ideal along the same stalk map.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_maximalIdeal_of_map_eq_zero: A ring homomorphism sends units to units. The given element maps to zero in a nonzero ring, where zero cannot be a unit. Hence it was a nonunit in the local source ring and belongs to its maximal ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.opensι_appLE_self_top_eq_topIso_inv: The section map from the ambient open to its entire open subscheme is the inverse of the canonical section identification. Both descriptions use restriction maps between the same opens, and parallel arrows of opens are equal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.spec_map_comp_fromSpecStalk_eq: Identify the two points and hence their stalk rings. The given transport becomes the identity and the ring maps agree. Applying spectra and composing with the canonical map from that stalk gives the same morphism on both sides.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.stalkIdeal_comap_chartPullbackPoint_eq: Each pulled-back ideal at the fiber-product point is the extension of the original stalk ideal along the corresponding stalk map. The two maps agree on scalars and modulo the maximal ideal. The fiber-product equations show that, in the coordinates of either chart, the maps differ only by shifting the distinguished coordinate by the difference of the two distinguished germs, with the sign chosen for that direction. This difference lies in both the maximal ideal and the maximal-contact stalk ideal. Maximal-contact invariance gives the required product containment with the derivative ideal on the stalk. Apply the coordinate-shift ideal comparison in both directions to get the two inclusions, hence equality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.stalkMap_germ_eq_zero_of_mem_ideal: Pull the section back to the affine open upstairs. It belongs to the pulled-back ideal by extension of section ideals. The closed subscheme defined by that ideal sends this section to zero. Passage to germs commutes with both section maps, so the composite on the original germ is also zero.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.subschemeι_appLE_eq_zero: The closed subscheme inclusion has the defining ideal as its kernel ideal. The section in that ideal therefore maps to zero on the inverse-image open. The section map on the indicated opens is this map followed by restriction, which preserves zero.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.ι_comp_eq_of_le: The inclusion of the smaller open factors through the inclusion of the larger one. Precompose the equality on the larger open with this factor map to obtain equality on the smaller open.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_common_charts_of_isMaxContactHype: The point of the order locus belongs to both hypersurfaces. Their maximal-contact charts show that each local hypersurface ideal is contained in the maximal-contact ideal. Choose a chart adapted to the first hypersurface and the common boundary, and shrink so every boundary coordinate retained in the assignment vanishes at the point. The first hypersurface occupies an index that no boundary member uses. On a common affine neighborhood take a principal generator of the second hypersurface. Since the second hypersurface also has normal crossings with the boundary, the differential of this generator has a coefficient nonzero at the point in a coordinate direction unused by the boundary. If its coefficient at the first hypersurface index already has this property, keep the current chart. Otherwise make a linear coordinate change in the unused direction so that the coefficient at the first hypersurface index is nonzero, preserving the first hypersurface coordinate and the boundary coordinates. The Jacobian replacement lemma then lets us shrink again and use the generator of the second hypersurface in the first hypersurface’s position, with all other coordinates shared. The two hypersurface coordinates generate their respective ideals and their germs lie in the maximal ideal because both hypersurfaces pass through the point. The earlier ideal containments survive restriction, giving maximal contact for both coordinates. The shared boundary assignment retains its injectivity and avoids the distinguished index.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.ideal_le_of_ideal_le_of_le: The larger affine section ring is Noetherian, so choose finitely many generators of the first section ideal there. Their restrictions generate the first ideal on the smaller affine open. Each generator belongs to the second ideal on the larger open by hypothesis, hence its restriction belongs to the second ideal on the smaller one. Thus the generated ideal is contained in the second ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.presheaf_map_mem_ideal_of_mem: The ideal of sections on the larger affine open maps into the ideal of sections on the smaller one under restriction. Applying this containment to the given section gives the result.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.restrictIdeal_eq_coordIdeal_of_coord_eq: On the affine open the given restricted ideal is generated by the indicated coordinate of the first chart. That section equals the indicated coordinate of the second chart, so the same principal ideal is generated in the second chart. The affine description of coordinate ideal sheaves gives the equality.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.appLE_opensι_top_eq_topIso_inv: The map of sections induced by the inclusion, from the ambient open to the whole open subscheme, uses the same restriction as the inverse section-ring identification. Any parallel restriction arrows between the two opens coincide, so the maps agree.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.basis_det_D_update_eq_coeff: Express the differentials in the given basis. The change-of-basis matrix is the identity except in the column for the replaced coordinate, where the column is the coefficient vector of the new differential. Expanding the determinant along this column, the only nonzero cofactor is the diagonal one, equal to one. Thus the determinant is the corresponding coefficient.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.coordIdeal_singleton_le_restrictIdeal_if: The affine open is identified with its own affine open subscheme, and the corresponding section-ring isomorphism identifies the chart’s single coordinate with the generator of its principal coordinate ideal. The restricted ideal on the whole open subscheme corresponds to the given section ideal under this isomorphism. Thus containment of the coordinate ideal implies membership of the original coordinate. Conversely, membership gives containment of the principal ideal on the whole affine open subscheme. Extending along restriction maps gives containment on its affine opens, hence containment of sheaves.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_isMaxContactCoord: Take an affine étale chart at the point and a section of the maximal-contact ideal whose germ lies in the maximal ideal outside its square. Its differential has nonzero image in the residue-field fiber by the cotangent argument. Write its differential in the basis of differentials of the original coordinates. Some coefficient has unit germ, since otherwise every term would vanish in the fiber. Shrink to the affine basic open where that coefficient is invertible. There replace the corresponding coordinate by the chosen section. The determinant relative to the original differential basis equals the invertible coefficient. The Jacobian criterion then gives an étale coordinate map, using finite presentation of the section algebra. The replacement belongs to the maximal-contact section ideal after restriction, so it is a maximal-contact coordinate. Its germ at the original point is the germ of the chosen section and lies in the maximal ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_section_maxContactIdeal_notMem_ma: The maximal-contact ideal has order one at the point. Its stalk is contained in the maximal ideal but lies outside containment in the square. On the affine open, the stalk ideal is generated by germs of sections of the section ideal. If all those germs belonged to the square, the whole stalk ideal would lie in the square and have order at least two. Thus some section has germ in the maximal ideal and outside its square.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isMaxContactCoord_iff: By definition a maximal-contact coordinate is one whose principal coordinate ideal lies in the restricted maximal-contact ideal. This is the stated equivalence.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isMaxContactCoord_iff_coord_mem: The maximal-contact condition is containment of the singleton coordinate ideal in the restricted maximal-contact ideal. On an affine open, such containment is equivalent to membership of its generator in the section ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isMaxContactCoord_one_iff: At mark one the maximal-contact ideal has derivative count zero and equals the original ideal. Substitute this into the coordinate containment that defines maximal contact.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.linearIndependent_one_tmul_D_of_notMem_m: The indicated element gives a nonzero cotangent class in the residue-field tensor of the maximal ideal, so this single vector is linearly independent. The conormal map to the residue-field fiber of the module of differentials is injective under the stated smoothness hypotheses. It sends the cotangent class to the indicated differential, preserving linear independence.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_support_maxContactIdeal_of_mem_order: For a positive mark, the support of the derivative iterate one below the mark is exactly the locus where the original order is at least the mark. The maximal-contact ideal is this iterate, so the given point is in its support.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.one_tmul_ne_zero_of_notMem_maximalIdeal_: Multiplication by any element of the maximal ideal sends the maximal ideal into its square, so it acts by zero on its cotangent quotient. Accordingly the quotient map to the cotangent space factors through the residue-field tensor product. It sends the indicated pure tensor to the class of the chosen element modulo the square. This class is nonzero by hypothesis, so the tensor is nonzero.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.orderAt_maxContactIdeal_eq_one: At a point where the ideal has the specified finite order, iterating derivatives through that many steps subtracts the number of steps from the order. The maximal-contact ideal uses one fewer step than the positive mark. Its order is therefore one.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.presheaf_map_op_eq_map_op: The category of opens is ordered by inclusion, so the two arrows with the same endpoints are equal. Their opposite arrows and their images under the presheaf are therefore equal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.stalkIdeal_maxContactIdeal_le_maximalIde: The maximal-contact ideal has order one at this point. The order criterion says its stalk lies in the first power of the maximal ideal, which is the maximal ideal itself.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.topIso_hom_comp_appLE_ι: The section map for the open inclusion on these opens is the inverse of the canonical section identification. Composing it with the forward identification therefore gives the identity.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.topIso_hom_comp_inv: The inverse and forward maps of the canonical section-ring isomorphism are mutually inverse. Taking the underlying ring maps gives the stated composition identity.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.topIso_inv_comp_hom: The forward map followed by its inverse is the identity on the domain. This equality of ring isomorphism composites gives the equality of their underlying ring maps.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.comap_comp_eq_of_comap_comap_eq: Pullback along a composite is successive pullback along its two maps. Rewrite each side this way and apply the given equality of successive pullbacks.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.comap_comp_ι_eq_comap_restrictIdeal: Restriction to the open is pullback along its inclusion. Pulling this restriction back along the given map is therefore pullback along the composite with the inclusion.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.comp_eq_of_lift_comp_eq: Use the two factorization identities to rewrite each composite out of the source through the further lift, followed by the same two inclusions. The given equality after those inclusions identifies the two rewritten composites.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_etale_equalizing_isMaxContactHype: At each point of the order locus, the local uniqueness result provides an affine étale comparison with both marked ideals, the boundary, and the maps on the maximal-contact subscheme identified. The globalization result combines such pointwise comparisons into the stated pair of étale maps covering the entire order locus.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_subscheme_comap_lift: The composite from the subscheme of the pulled-back ideal to the original target kills the original ideal, because its pullback vanishes on the subscheme by construction. It therefore factors through the closed subscheme defined by the original ideal. The factorization gives the asserted morphism.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.nonempty_etaleMaxContactComparison: Choose a common affine neighborhood with two étale charts for the two hypersurfaces. They agree on all coordinates except the distinguished one, and the boundary ideals use only the other coordinates or are unit ideals. Form the fiber product of the chart maps over affine space. The local comparison for maximal-contact coordinates gives a point above the original point and a neighborhood where the two pulled-back ideals have equal stalks. It also identifies the two hypersurface pullbacks and shows that the projections agree on the maximal-contact subscheme there. Shrink this neighborhood to an affine basic open containing the point. The projections followed by the original open inclusion are étale and have the same structure map to the field. Equality of the pulled-back ideals on the smaller open follows from stalk equality. The boundary pullbacks agree by the shared coordinate descriptions and the fiber-product equations. Smooth pullback identifies the maximal-contact ideal of the common pulled-back input with the pullback of the original maximal-contact ideal. The corresponding smaller closed subscheme factors through the open part of the original comparison subscheme where the projections agree, so they still agree on it. These data give the required comparison.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.range_base_subset_range_preimage_ι: At any point of the source, the image under the map to the closed subscheme has ambient image equal to the image through the map with range contained in the given open. Thus the point lies in the inverse image of that open. This is the range of its open inclusion.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.IsMaxContactHypersurface.orderAtLeastLoc: Take a point of the stated order locus and a neighborhood from the maximal-contact condition. The neighborhood cannot be disjoint from that locus. Thus the hypersurface is defined there by a maximal-contact coordinate. This coordinate belongs to the maximal-contact ideal, so the principal section ideal of the hypersurface lies in that ideal. Extending to the stalk preserves the inclusion. The maximal-contact ideal has a proper stalk at every point of the order locus, so the hypersurface stalk is also proper. Hence the point belongs to the hypersurface support.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isMaxContactHypersurface_iff: The definition requires an affine neighborhood at every point. Either the neighborhood avoids the order locus and the hypersurface is absent there, or the hypersurface is defined by a maximal-contact coordinate of an étale chart. Expanding the definition gives the equivalence.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.IsDerivBalanced.derivIdealSheafIterate_p: Apply the derivative-balance condition to the given index, using that it lies below the mark.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isDerivBalanced_iff: Derivative balance is defined by the displayed comparison of ideal powers for every derivative order below the mark. Expanding the definition gives both directions.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isDerivBalanced_of_pow_le: The assumed inequalities are exactly those in the definition of derivative balance.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isDerivBalanced_one: The only nonnegative index below one is zero. Zero iterations leave the ideal unchanged, and both powers in the required inequality then have exponent one. The ideals are equal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isMaxContactInvariant_of_mul_le: The definition of maximal-contact invariance is the stated containment of the product of the maximal-contact ideal and the first derivative ideal. Thus the given containment proves the property.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.maxContactIdeal_eq_derivIdealSheafIterat: The maximal-contact ideal is defined by iterating the derivative ideal one fewer time than the mark, using truncated subtraction at zero. This is the stated identity.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.maxContactIdeal_ideal: The maximal-contact ideal is the derivative iterate one below the mark. Evaluating a derivative iterate on an affine open gives the same iterate of the section ideal over the induced section algebra. Apply that evaluation formula.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.maxContactIdeal_one: For mark one the defining derivative count is zero. Zero iterations leave the original ideal unchanged.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.comap_maxContactIdeal_le_exceptionalIdea: The given exceptional factorization identifies the upstairs ideal with the controlled transform by uniqueness. The maximal-contact ideal is the derivative iterate one below the mark. Apply the pullback bound for this number of derivatives. The remaining exceptional exponent is one, and the upstairs derivative iterate is the upstairs maximal-contact ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_etaleChart_of_isMaxContactHypersu: Take a neighborhood from the maximal-contact hypothesis. If it already gives a coordinate chart for the hypersurface, use it. Otherwise the hypersurface ideal is the unit ideal on the neighborhood. Choose a smaller étale chart there. The unit ideal remains the unit ideal after restriction.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.idealSheafData_eq_of_forall_ideal_eq: An ideal sheaf is determined by its section ideals on affine opens. The given equalities identify all these section ideals, giving equality of sheaves.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.inStrictNormalCrossingPosition_singleton: Around every point the hypersurface ideal is either absent or generated by a single coordinate on an étale chart. This proves that it is a smooth divisor. The same charts establish the pointwise normal crossings condition for the one-entry list by assigning no coordinate in the first case and that coordinate in the second. With one entry the distinctness condition is automatic.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isMaxContactHypersurfaceAt_strictTransfo: Choose a blowup chart containing the point and then an affine neighborhood inside it. On the chart the exceptional ideal is generated locally by a nonzerodivisor. The hypersurface ideal downstairs lies in the maximal-contact ideal, so its total transform lies in the exceptional ideal times the upstairs maximal-contact ideal by the derivative bound. If the hypersurface index is the exceptional index, its total transform is exactly that exceptional ideal and its strict transform is empty on the chart. Canceling the exceptional ideal in the containment forces the upstairs maximal-contact ideal to be the unit ideal there. Thus the chart avoids the transformed order locus. If the indices differ, the total transform is the exceptional ideal times the corresponding upstairs coordinate ideal, which is the strict-transform ideal. Cancellation shows this coordinate ideal lies in the upstairs maximal-contact ideal. Restricting to the chosen affine neighborhood gives the required chart in either case.

At the image center point, the original order reaches the threshold and the hypersurface ideal is contained in the center ideal. Choose affine coordinates for the smooth center and a coordinate description of the smooth hypersurface. Its defining coordinate is a linear combination of the center coordinates with some coefficient nonzero at the point. Replace the corresponding center coordinate by that linear combination on a smaller chart. This gives an étale chart and preserves the center ideal because the chosen coefficient is now a unit. The selected coordinate generates the hypersurface ideal. Shrink again into a neighborhood where the hypersurface ideal lies in the maximal-contact ideal, so the new coordinate belongs to it. Apply the local blowup-chart result to these coordinates.

Choose a downstairs maximal-contact neighborhood and shrink it off the center. There the strict transform equals the total transform. If the hypersurface is absent downstairs and the neighborhood is disjoint from the order locus, its pullback remains absent. The transformed order locus maps into the original order locus, so its inverse-image neighborhood avoids the transformed order locus. In the other case the blowup is an isomorphism on the neighborhood, and the downstairs chart transfers to an étale chart upstairs. The strict transform is given by its corresponding coordinate. The pullback of the downstairs maximal-contact ideal is contained in the upstairs one by the exceptional-factor bound and containment of a product in its second factor. Hence the transferred coordinate has maximal contact. Take an affine neighborhood upstairs inside the open in either case.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isMaxContactHypersurface_strictTransform: Local Noetherianity upstairs supplies the quasi-compactness of the strict-transform inclusion. The general strict-transform theorem applies with the stated center and exceptional factorization hypotheses, yielding the maximal-contact condition upstairs.

The blowup is smooth over the field by the normal crossings condition. The center order hypothesis gives the containment of the input ideal in the center power at the mark. At each point upstairs apply the local maximal-contact result over the center or the local result away from it, according to the image point. These neighborhoods prove the global maximal-contact condition.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.le_center_of_isMaxContactHypersurface: The center support lies in the order locus, which lies in the hypersurface support by maximal contact. The hypersurface support is the order locus at threshold one. Apply the strict normal crossings power criterion at exponent one to obtain containment of the hypersurface ideal in the center ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_orderAtLeastLocus_base_of_mem_orderA: Suppose the image point has order at most one below the mark. The input ideal is contained in the center power at the mark and hence at the lower exponent. Multiplying the given transformed ideal by one exceptional factor gives the controlled transform at that lower exponent, by the total-transform identity and uniqueness. The controlled-transform order bound now gives order at most one below the mark for this product at the upstairs point. The transformed ideal contains this product, so its order is at most the product’s order. This contradicts membership in the upstairs order locus.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mul_le_left_idealSheafData: At each point, a product of elements of the two stalk ideals belongs to the first ideal because it is an ideal in the stalk ring. Thus their product ideal lies in the first stalk ideal. Stalkwise containment gives the sheaf containment.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mul_le_right_idealSheafData: At each point the stalk of the product is the product of the two stalk ideals. Every product of generators belongs to the second stalk ideal because it is closed under multiplication by elements of the local ring. This gives containment at each stalk and hence containment of sheaves.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.pullbackChartIso_coordIdeal: The transported chart map is the restricted blowup isomorphism followed by the original chart map. Its coordinate ideal is the pullback from affine space along that composite, which is successive pullback along the original chart map and the isomorphism.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.restrictIdeal_le_of_le_opens: Restriction to the smaller open equals restriction to the larger open followed by pullback along the intervening open inclusion. Pullback preserves containment, so the given inclusion restricts to the smaller open.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.restrictIdeal_strictTransform_eq_of_coma: Strict transform commutes with restriction to the indicated open. There its defining saturation uses the pulled-back center, which is the unit ideal by hypothesis. Saturation by the unit leaves the pulled-back divisor ideal unchanged. This is the restriction of its total transform.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.saturation_of_eq_top: On every affine open the saturating ideal is generated by the unit one. A section belongs to its saturation precisely when some power of one times the section belongs to the input ideal. This condition is just ordinary membership. The section ideals therefore agree on all affine opens.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_mem_mul_mem_of_map_le: Choose finitely many generators of the first ideal. For each generator, membership of its image in the extended second ideal gives a fraction with numerator in the second ideal. Clear the denominator and then a further multiplier from the multiplicative set to obtain membership downstairs. Multiply the resulting multipliers for all generators. This product still lies in the multiplicative set and sends each generator into the second ideal, so it sends the whole first ideal there.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_notMem_mul_mem_of_map_le: The element’s image belongs to the extended second ideal. Write it as a fraction with numerator in that ideal and denominator outside the prime. Cross-multiply and use another element outside the prime to make the equality hold downstairs. The product of these two multipliers is outside the prime by primality and sends the given element into the second ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_opens_stalkIdeal_eq: Choose an affine neighborhood and view the two equal stalk ideals as extensions of their section ideals to the localization at the point. The section ideals are finitely generated by Noetherianity. Clear denominators on generators in each direction to find two multipliers outside the point prime, one sending each ideal into the other. Their product stays outside the prime and has the same two membership properties. On its basic open the product is invertible in every stalk. Canceling it after extension in both directions proves equality of the two stalk ideals throughout this neighborhood.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.ideal_eq_of_stalkIdeal_eq: Stalk equality on the affine open gives stalk containment in both directions. Apply the section-ideal containment result twice to obtain equality of the section ideals.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.ideal_le_of_stalkIdeal_le: Each maximal ideal of the affine section ring corresponds to a point of the affine open. There the given stalk containment is containment after localizing at that maximal ideal. For each section of the first ideal, clearing denominators gives a multiplier outside that maximal ideal taking the section into the second ideal. The maximal-ideal criterion for containment yields the desired inclusion of section ideals.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.le_of_forall_isMaximal_exists_mul_mem: Suppose an element of the first ideal lies outside the second. The multipliers that send it into the second ideal form an ideal. This ideal is proper because it excludes one, so choose a maximal ideal containing it. The hypothesis gives a multiplier outside that maximal ideal sending the element into the second ideal, contrary to the containment of all such multipliers.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.map_le_map_of_isUnit_mul_mem: For each element of the first ideal, the image of its product with the multiplier belongs to the extended second ideal. Multiplying by the inverse of the image of the multiplier shows that the image of the original element belongs to that ideal. These images generate the extended first ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.notMem_of_mem_primeCompl: The prime complement is the multiplicative set of elements outside the prime. Membership in it therefore says the element does not belong to the prime.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.restrictIdeal_eq_of_stalkIdeal_eq: Every affine open of the open subscheme has an affine image in the original scheme, contained in the chosen open. The two ideals have equal stalks there by hypothesis, so their section ideals on this image agree. Pullback along the inclusion extends these equal section ideals to the corresponding affine open of the open subscheme. Hence the restricted ideal sheaves agree on every affine open.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdealIterate_mul_derivIdeal_tunedId: One fewer derivative step than the positive threshold is bounded by the tuned ideal at threshold one. A single derivative step is bounded by the tuned ideal at the threshold decreased by one. Multiplying these two bounds and applying the product rule adds the thresholds back to the original threshold.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdealIterate_succ_mul_tuningMonomia: Removing a copy of the factor at the chosen index reduces the total weight by its weight. If the next derivative index is still below the mark, adding one factor there raises the total by one less than the removed weight, so the new monomial loses exactly one unit of weight and qualifies at the desired threshold. If the next index is at least the mark, the removed weight was one. The remaining monomial already qualifies, and multiplying it by any ideal stays inside it.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdealIterate_tunedIdeal_le: Induct on the derivative count. Zero steps leave the ideal unchanged. At the next step, use monotonicity to differentiate the induction bound. If the threshold remaining in that bound is positive, the one-step estimate reduces it by one. If it is zero, the new target is still the unit ideal. Both cases give the bound with truncated subtraction.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdeal_one: The multiplicative identity for ideals is the unit ideal. The derivative ideal contains its input, so the derivative of the unit ideal is still the unit ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdeal_tunedIdeal_succ_le: The derivative of the supremum lies in the supremum of the derivatives of its contributing terms. For each qualifying monomial, the unchanged product qualifies at the preceding threshold. The Leibniz terms replace one factor by its next derivative, which lowers the weight by at most one under the monomial estimate. Thus all required terms are contained in the tuned ideal at the preceding threshold.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_ne_zero_of_one_le_tuningWeight: If every exponent in the range were zero, all weighted contributions would vanish and the total weight would be zero. This contradicts the positive lower bound.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.listProd_map_range_eq_prod: The empty range gives the identity for both products. Increasing the range by one appends the same factor to the list product and to the finite-set product, so induction gives equality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_of_natCast_add_one_mul_mem: The positive integer coefficient is nonzero in the rationals, so its image in the rational algebra is a unit with inverse the image of its rational reciprocal. Multiplying the given ideal element by this inverse shows the original element belongs to the ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mul_derivIdeal_prod_le: Induct on the number of factors in the product. The empty product has unit derivative ideal, giving the first hypothesis directly. For a nonempty product, the Leibniz estimate bounds its derivative by the sum of the terms from differentiating the last factor and from differentiating the earlier product. In the last-factor term, exponent zero leaves the product unchanged and the first hypothesis applies. A positive exponent is reduced by one and accompanied by the next derivative ideal, by the power derivative estimate. This is one of the terms covered by the second hypothesis. For the earlier-product term, absorb the last factor into the fixed multiplier and apply induction. The hypotheses for the shorter product follow from the original ones because changes at earlier indices leave the last exponent unchanged. Adding the two containments gives the result.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mul_sup_le: An element of the sum of the two ideals is a sum of one element from each. Multiplying by an element of the common factor distributes over this sum. Both products belong to the target ideal by hypothesis, so their sum also belongs. Such products generate the left-hand ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mul_tunedIdeal_le_iff: The tuned ideal is the supremum of its qualifying monomial ideals. Multiplication by the fixed ideal distributes over this supremum. The resulting supremum is contained in the target exactly when every product term is contained there.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.pow_mul_mem_derivIdeal_tunedIdeal_succ: Induct on the additional index in the bound. If it is zero, the derivative count already reaches the successor threshold. The principal-power product bound puts the element in that successor-threshold ideal and hence in its derivative ideal. In the inductive case, the product with one extra power of the contact element lies in the successor-threshold ideal. Its derivative therefore lies in the desired derivative ideal. The Leibniz rule expresses this derivative as the requested product times the positive integer one above the derivative count, plus the extra-power product of the derivative of the given element. The latter product lies in the target by induction, since the differentiated element belongs to the next derivative iterate and the increased count preserves the required bound. Subtract it and divide by the positive integer, which is a unit in the rational algebra.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.pow_mul_mem_tunedIdeal: The derivative iterate of the tuned ideal lies in the tuned ideal with threshold reduced by the derivative count. Multiplying by the specified power of the maximal-contact element raises that threshold by the exponent, by the principal-power product bound.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.prod_derivIdealIterate_pow_pow: Powers of a finite product in a commutative monoid distribute over its factors. A power of each individual ideal power multiplies the exponents. Reorder the two integer factors of the exponent to obtain the formula.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.span_pow_mul_tunedIdeal_le: Distribute the product with the principal power over the monomials qualifying for the original tuned ideal. The monomial estimate bounds each product by the tuned ideal at its weight plus the power. This threshold is at least the original threshold plus the power, so monotonicity gives the required bound.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.span_pow_mul_tuningMonomial_le: The given element belongs to the derivative ideal one below the mark. Its specified power therefore generates an ideal contained in the same power of that derivative ideal, which is a tuning monomial supported at this single index. That index has weight one. Multiplying by the original monomial adds the power to its weight, so the product is contained in the tuned ideal at the increased threshold.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tunedIdeal_antitone: Every exponent function admitted by the higher threshold also satisfies the lower threshold. The corresponding monomial is contained in the tuned ideal for the lower threshold. Take the supremum over the higher threshold.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tunedIdeal_eq_iSup: By definition the tuned ideal is the supremum of all tuning monomial ideals whose weights reach the stated threshold. The displayed supremum enumerates precisely those terms.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tunedIdeal_le_derivIdeal_tunedIdeal_succ: Take an element of the tuned ideal as an element of its zeroth derivative iterate. Apply the principal-power induction with derivative count zero and additional index equal to the successor threshold. The resulting zeroth power is one, so the given element belongs to the derivative of the successor-threshold tuned ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tunedIdeal_le_iff: Containment of the supremum implies containment of each contributing ideal. Conversely, if all ideals with qualifying weight lie in the target, their supremum lies there as well.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tunedIdeal_mul_le: Multiplication of ideals distributes over suprema, so it suffices to multiply one contributing monomial from each tuned ideal. Their product is the monomial with the pointwise sum of exponents. Its weight is the sum of their weights, hence at least the sum of the thresholds. The product is therefore contained in the target tuned ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tunedIdeal_one_le_derivIdealIterate: Every monomial qualifying at threshold one has a nonzero exponent at some index in the range. The product is contained in that factor, and its positive power is contained in the corresponding derivative iterate. This derivative index is at most one below the mark. Monotonicity of derivative iterations puts the factor in the iterate one below the mark. Hence every contributing monomial lies in that iterate.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tunedIdeal_zero: The zero exponent function qualifies at threshold zero. Its product is the unit ideal, so the tuned ideal contains the unit ideal and is therefore equal to it.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tuningMonomial_eq_derivIdealIterate_mul_: Separate the factor at the chosen index in each monomial. All other factors agree. The exponent at that index increases by one, so the changed factor is the original factor multiplied by the corresponding derivative iterate.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tuningMonomial_eq_prod: The tuning monomial is defined as the product of the indicated powers of the derivative iterates. This gives the stated formula.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tuningMonomial_le_tunedIdeal: Since the exponent function meets the weight threshold, its monomial ideal occurs among the ideals defining the tuned ideal. Each such ideal is contained in their supremum.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tuningMonomial_mul: The sum of the two exponent functions adds their values at each index. The product formula therefore gives the monomial for that sum.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tuningMonomial_mul_fun_add: Group factors with the same derivative index from the two products. Commutativity allows the grouping, and multiplying the corresponding powers adds their exponents. This gives the product for the pointwise sum.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tuningMonomial_pow: Natural-number scalar multiplication scales the exponent function at each index. The monomial for this function is the stated power by the product-of-powers formula.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tuningMonomial_pow_fun_mul: Expand the monomial as its product of derivative powers. Taking a power distributes over this finite product and multiplies each exponent by the power, giving the monomial for the scaled function.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tuningMonomial_single: Each factor away from the selected index has exponent zero and equals the unit ideal. At the selected index the exponent is one, so the product gives that derivative iterate.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tuningMonomial_zero: Every exponent is zero, so each factor is the unit ideal. Their product is the unit ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tuningWeight_add: Addition of exponent functions is pointwise. The weight of their sum is therefore the sum of their weights by the weighted-sum addition rule.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tuningWeight_eq_add_sub_of_succ: Separate the contribution at the chosen index from each weighted sum. The remaining terms are unchanged. The exponent at the chosen index is larger by one in the first function, so its contribution is larger by exactly the weight of that index.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tuningWeight_eq_sum: The tuning weight is defined by summing each exponent below the mark multiplied by the mark minus its index. This is the displayed sum.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tuningWeight_fun_add: Distribute multiplication by each weight over the sum of the two exponents. Summing and grouping the contributions of the two exponent functions gives the two separate weights.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tuningWeight_mul_left: Each exponent is multiplied by the same scalar. Move that scalar outside each weighted term and then outside the finite sum, giving the corresponding multiple of the original weight.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tuningWeight_nsmul: Natural-number scalar multiplication of exponent functions multiplies every exponent by that number. Apply the rule for pulling a common scalar out of the weighted sum.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tuningWeight_single: Only the chosen index has a nonzero exponent, namely one. Its contribution to the weighted sum is the mark minus that index.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdealIterate_tunedIdeal_pow_le: The derivative iterate is contained in the tuned ideal whose threshold is the original threshold minus the derivative count. Raise this containment to the original threshold and use the general product bound for powers of a tuned ideal. This puts the result inside the tuned ideal at the product of the two thresholds. The difference is positive by the index hypothesis, so the equality for powers of the original tuned ideal rewrites this final bound as the asserted power.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_le_tuningWeight_eq_mul: Induct on the requested number of blocks of weight equal to the common multiple. The zero function gives the zero-block case. In a positive case the total weight is at least the number of available indices times the common multiple, so the list of indices is nonempty. If every individual contribution were smaller than the common multiple, their sum would be at most the number of indices times one less than that multiple, a contradiction. Choose an index making a contribution at least the common multiple. Its weight divides the common multiple, so take exactly the number of copies needed at that index. There are enough copies because the index’s total contribution is large enough. Removing these copies reduces the tuning weight by one block and leaves the lower bound required by the induction hypothesis. Restore the removed block to the smaller selection obtained by induction. The selection stays within the original exponents and has exactly the requested weight.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tunedIdeal_mul_eq_tunedIdeal_add: The product rule gives one inclusion. For the reverse, take a monomial contributing to the ideal at the sum threshold. Its weight is large enough to select a subexponent of the first threshold exactly, by the block selection result and the lower bound on the second threshold. The remaining exponents have weight at least the second threshold by additivity. The original monomial ideal is the product belonging to these two exponent functions. Each lies in the corresponding tuned ideal, giving the reverse inclusion.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tunedIdeal_pow_eq_tunedIdeal_mul: Induct on the positive power, where the case of power one is immediate. For the next power, the induction hypothesis gives the tuned ideal at the previous multiplied threshold. This threshold is at least the lower bound required by the product equality, because the preceding exponent is positive and the original threshold is large enough. Multiplying by the original tuned ideal adds one more copy of the threshold, proving the equality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tunedIdeal_pow_le: At exponent zero the zeroth power and the tuned ideal at weight zero are both the unit ideal. At a successor, multiply the induction containment by the original tuned ideal. The product rule adds the weight thresholds, giving the threshold equal to the next exponent times the original threshold.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tuningWeight_ite: Only the term at the chosen index contributes to the weighted sum, because all other exponent entries are zero. That term is the given exponent times its weight.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tuningWeight_sub: The pointwise difference plus the smaller exponent function recovers the larger exponent function. The tuning weight is an additive weighted sum, so the weight of the difference plus the smaller weight is the larger weight. Subtracting gives the desired equality.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdealSheafIterate_pow_le_tunedSheaf: Evaluate on an arbitrary affine open. The power of the derivative iterate becomes the corresponding power of the ring-level iterate, and the tuned sheaf becomes the tuned ring ideal. The latter contains the monomial with nonzero exponent only at the derivative index one below the mark, giving the asserted containment.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdealSheaf_tunedSheaf_succ: On each affine open the ring-level derivative bound puts the derivative of the successor-threshold tuned ideal in the preceding tuned ideal. For the reverse inclusion, work on stalks. At a point of maximal order, choose a maximal-contact coordinate. It belongs to the required original derivative ideal, and its coordinate derivation sends it to one. The ring-level reverse containment using this derivation applies on the chart and hence on the stalk. At a point of smaller order, the original derivative iterate one below the mark has unit stalk. The successor-threshold tuned sheaf contains a power of that iterate and so has unit stalk as well. Its derivative then has unit stalk. This gives the reverse containment at every point.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.ideal_listProd_map: For the empty list, global evaluation on the affine open gives the unit section ideal. For a nonempty list, evaluation preserves the product of the first factor with the tail product. Applying induction to the tail gives the desired product of section ideals.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.ideal_map_prod_range: Extension along the ring map preserves multiplication and the unit ideal. Applying this property successively to the finite product over the range gives the product of the extended ideals.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.ideal_prod_derivIdealSheafIterate_pow: Evaluating on the affine open preserves the product and every power. Each derivative sheaf iterate evaluates to the derivative iterate of the section ideal. These evaluated factors in range order are exactly the product defining the tuning monomial in the section ring.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isMaxContactInvariantTunedSheaf: Check the product containment on each affine open. Evaluation preserves the product, and the differentiated tuned sheaves evaluate to the corresponding derivatives of the tuned section ideal. The ring-level maximal-contact invariance estimate for this tuned ideal gives the containment on every affine open.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.map_tunedIdeal_basicOpen: Restriction to the basic open extends the original affine section ideal to the section ideal there. The same is true for each derivative sheaf iterate. Thus extension along the restriction map commutes with the ring derivative iterates of this ideal. The compatibility of tuning with such extension gives the required ideal on the basic open.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.map_tunedIdeal_of_map_derivIdealIterate: The exponent functions meeting the weight condition are the same in both rings. Each product term downstairs extends to the corresponding term upstairs because derivative iterates, powers, and products commute with extension here. Every extended term lies in the tuned ideal upstairs, proving one containment. Conversely each qualifying term upstairs is such an extension and therefore lies in the extension of the tuned ideal downstairs.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.map_tuningMonomial_of_map_derivIdealIter: Expand the tuning monomial as the product of powers of derivative iterates. Ideal extension preserves the product and each power. The assumed compatibility with every derivative iterate identifies each extended factor with the corresponding factor for the extended ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.maxContactIdealTunedSheafEq: A derivative step of a positive-threshold tuned sheaf lowers the threshold by one. Induction gives the tuned sheaf at the original threshold minus the number of steps, as long as the steps do not exceed the threshold. Performing one fewer step than the positive threshold leaves threshold one, where the tuned sheaf equals the derivative iterate one below the original mark.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.pow_derivIdealIterate_pred_le_tunedIdeal: Use the exponent function that is zero except at the derivative index one below the mark, where it has the given exponent. This index has weight one, so the term meets the threshold exactly. Its product is the requested power of that derivative iterate.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tunedSheaf_ideal: The tuned ring ideals on affine opens are compatible with basic-open restriction and thus form an ideal sheaf. Each qualifying product of derivative sheaves evaluates to a tuning monomial on each open, which is contained in the local tuned ring ideal. Taking the supremum gives one inclusion. Conversely, every qualifying tuning monomial in the section ring is the evaluation of a product appearing in the definition of the tuned sheaf. These monomials generate the local tuned ring ideal, proving the reverse inclusion.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tunedSheaf_one_eq_derivIdealSheafIterate: On affine sections, the tuned ideal at threshold one is contained in the derivative ideal one below the mark by the ring-level threshold-one estimate. Conversely, the first power of that iterate is one of the qualifying tuned monomials. These inclusions give equality of sheaves.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.CoSupportTunedSheafEqAndOrderLE.orderLE: The assumed property supplies both equality of the order loci and the pointwise order bound at the given positive threshold. Take its order-bound conclusion.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.balancedTunedSheaf_eq: The balanced construction is defined by choosing the tuning exponent of the mark as the threshold of the tuned sheaf. The identity follows by substitution.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.lcmUpTo_eq_foldr: The common multiple is defined by taking the least common multiple successively over the list of integers from one through the bound, starting with one. This is the stated formula.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.lcmUpTo_one: At bound one the list contains only one. Taking the least common multiple of this entry and the initial value one gives one.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.orderLE_iff: The order bound on the ideal sheaf is defined by requiring the same bound at every point of the scheme. This gives the equivalence.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tunedSheaf_eq_iSup: The tuned sheaf is defined as the supremum of products of derivative ideal powers whose exponent functions have weight at least the threshold. The displayed sum assigns weight equal to the mark minus the derivative index, which gives exactly the defining supremum.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tuningExponent_of_le_one: For a mark at most one, the first case of the definition applies and assigns exponent one.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tuningExponent_of_two_le: A mark of at least two is above one. The definition therefore selects the product of one less than the mark and the least common multiple up to the mark.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tuningExponent_one: The mark one satisfies the case for marks at most one, so its tuning exponent is one.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.balancedTunedSheaf_comap: Both balanced tuned sheaves use the tuning exponent of the same mark, so their thresholds agree. The smooth pullback identity for tuned sheaves at that threshold gives the claim.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.balancedTunedSheaf_eq_top_of_orderAtLeas: The balanced tuned sheaf uses the prescribed tuning exponent as its threshold. Apply the empty-order-locus argument at this threshold to obtain the unit ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.balancedTunedSheaf_one: The balanced tuning exponent at mark one is one. The balanced sheaf therefore agrees with the tuned sheaf of mark and threshold one, which equals the original ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.extendExponentsByZero_apply_of_lt: An index below the cutoff belongs to the finite index set. At such an index, extension by zero returns the original exponent.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.idealSheafData_pow_antitone_of_le: On an affine open, evaluation of a power gives the corresponding power of its section ideal. An ideal’s higher power is contained in its lower power, since the higher power is the lower one times an ideal. The affine inclusions give the sheaf inclusion.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.idealSheafData_pow_le_self: On each affine open the power of the sheaf gives the same power of the section ideal. A positive power of a ring ideal lies in that ideal because it contains the ideal as a factor. Apply this on each affine open.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.le_sum_mul_min_of_le_sum: If all exponents in the sum are already at most the threshold, truncating them changes nothing. Otherwise, an exponent above the threshold becomes exactly the threshold when truncated. Its weight is at least one because its index is below the mark, so that term alone contributes at least the threshold. All other terms are nonnegative.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.listProd_map_le_listProd_map: For the empty list both products are the unit ideal. For a nonempty list, apply the pointwise containment to its first entry and use induction on the tail. Monotonicity of multiplication combines these two inclusions.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.listProd_map_range_one: The range list of length one contains only zero. Its mapped product is the indicated value at zero multiplied by the empty product, so it equals that value.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mul_le_mul_idealSheafData: On each affine open, the section ideal of a product is the product of the section ideals. Monotonicity of ideal multiplication gives the desired inclusion on each open, hence on the sheaves.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.prod_pow_derivIdealSheafIterate_le_tuned: The exponent function satisfies the required weight bound. Its product is therefore one of the ideals in the supremum defining the tuned sheaf, and lies in that supremum.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tunedSheaf_comap: Use the bounded exponent presentation on both schemes. Smooth pullback commutes with each derivative iterate and preserves powers of ideal sheaves, so it carries each downstairs factor to the corresponding factor upstairs. It also preserves products and the supremum over the same bounded exponent vectors. Thus pullback gives exactly the tuned sheaf of the pulled-back ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tunedSheaf_eq_iSup_fin: For a term in the original supremum, truncate every exponent in the finite range at the threshold. The weighted sum remains large enough by the truncation estimate. Lowering an ideal’s exponent enlarges its power, so the original product lies in the product for the resulting bounded exponent vector. This proves containment in the bounded supremum. Conversely every bounded exponent vector extends by zero to an exponent function admitted in the original supremum, so each bounded term occurs there.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tunedSheaf_eq_top_of_orderAtLeastLocus_e: Absence of points of order at least the mark implies that the derivative iterate one below the mark is the unit ideal. Choose the exponent function supported only at that derivative index with value equal to the threshold. That index has weight one, so its product is admitted. The selected factor and all zero-exponent factors are unit ideals, so their product is the unit ideal. The supremum is therefore the unit ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tunedSheaf_one_one: With mark one the only derivative order in a product is zero, with weight one. An admitted exponent is therefore at least one, and the corresponding ideal power is contained in the original ideal. Choosing exponent one gives the original ideal itself as a term in the supremum, proving equality.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_affineOpen_mem: Affine opens cover a scheme, so the given point lies in at least one of them.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_tuningExponent_eq: At mark one, take both multipliers to be one. For a mark of at least two, the tuning exponent is one less than the mark times the least common multiple up to that mark. Use one less than the mark as the first multiplier. Since the mark divides that positive common multiple, the quotient is positive. Multiplying that quotient by one less than the mark gives the second positive multiplier.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isMarked_iff_balanced_tunedSheaf: Write the tuning exponent both as a positive multiple of the mark and as an appropriate multiple of the least common multiple up to the mark. The first expression puts the balanced ideal between the corresponding power of the input and the tuned bound, by the power containment and the definition of the balanced ideal. Applying the marked-sequence comparison gives the marking equivalence and equality of order loci along the sequence. The tuning exponent is positive, so maximal-contact invariance follows from the invariance theorem. The second expression meets the hypotheses of the derivative-balance bound, giving the remaining inequalities.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isMarked_iff_of_pow_le_of_le_tunedSheaf: Assume the sequence is marked for the first ideal. Its smooth centers and strict normal crossings condition give the hypotheses of the induction for comparing transforms. The marked center condition of the first ideal supplies the center inclusion at each stage. Equality of the order loci and the exceptional factorizations from that induction then give the marking conditions for the second ideal. Conversely, assume it is marked for the second ideal.
